chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Sindi, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ibrahim ibn Mihzam al-Asadi, from Abu Hamzah, from Ali ibn al-Hussein (peace be upon them both), who said:

Indeed, the tongue of the son of Adam overlooks his limbs every day and says to them: 'How have you fared?' They reply: 'We are fine if you leave us alone.' And they say: 'God, God [is our witness] concerning us,' and they implore him, and they say: 'We are rewarded because of you, and we are punished because of you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between the tongue and the limbs according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq employs this vivid anthropomorphic imagery to highlight the tongue's hierarchical authority over the other limbs, a concept rooted in Shia ethical teachings on self-accountability (muhasaba). The narration underscores the theological principle that the tongue serves as the primary instrument for both spiritual merit and sin, thereby linking physical actions to divine recompense.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 1-15 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash’ari, on the authority of Ali ibn al-Hikam, on the authority of Ibrahim ibn Mihzam Al-Asady, on the authority of Abi Hamzih, on the authority of Ali ibn al-Hussein (MGB), “

Man’s tongue addresses his other organs everyday and asks them how they are. They reply that ‘we would be fine if you left us alone’. They swear by God and ask it to remember God in regards to them. They say that they get rewarded due to it, and they also get punished due to it.”
